body_md: `From<T>` builds one type from another; `Into<T>` is the automatic flip side. Implement `From` once and `into()` works free via the blanket impl. Use `value.into()` when the target type is known from context.
hook: Implement From once, get Into for free — here is how.

quiz.explain: A From impl gives you Into automatically through the blanket impl.
options: From gives Into automatically
Into gives From automatically
Both must be written by hand
Neither can convert types
quiz.q: If you implement From<A> for B, what do you get?

takeaway: Implement From for conversions and rely on Into for ergonomic call sites.
trap: Implementing both From and Into manually causes conflicting-impl errors.

body_md: `Debug` (`{:?}`) is for developers with derived output. `Display` (`{}`) is for users and must be written by hand. Derive Debug always, implement Display for messages, errors, and pretty CLI output.
hook: Derive Debug, hand-write Display — know which is which.

quiz.explain: Debug is developer-facing and derivable while Display is user-facing and manual.
options: Display is derivable; Debug is manual
They are interchangeable formatters
Debug is for devs; Display for users
Debug prints in release builds only
quiz.q: How do Debug and Display differ?

takeaway: Derive Debug for diagnostics and implement Display for user-facing output.
trap: Using Debug output in user interfaces leaks internals and looks unpolished.

body_md: `Deref` lets `Box<String>` act like `&str` via **deref coercion**. Method calls auto-borrow through the chain. Implement `Deref` for smart pointers, never just to save keystrokes on normal structs.
hook: Why does Box<String> have string methods? Deref coercion.

quiz.explain: Deref coercion follows Deref impls (&Box<String> to &String to &str) so smart pointers act like their target.
options: Clones the inner value on access
Turns &Box<String> into &str for you
Moves the inner value out of the Box
Calls Clone to get the target type
quiz.q: What does deref coercion do?

takeaway: Rely on deref coercion for smart pointers but avoid abusing it elsewhere.
trap: Implementing Deref on domain types hides ownership and confuses method resolution.

body_md: `Cow<'a, str>` holds borrowed **or** owned text. Return borrowed when no edit is needed, owned only when you must allocate. Call `.into_owned()` or `.to_mut()` at the boundary that needs ownership.
hook: Borrow when you can, own when you must — Cow does both.

quiz.explain: Cow avoids allocation on the common borrowed path and owns only when needed.
options: No allocation when nothing changes
It always clones, so callers own it
It's faster to hash than a String
It stores text on the stack instead
quiz.q: Why return Cow instead of String?

takeaway: Return Cow to avoid allocation when the borrowed fast path suffices.
trap: Calling into_owned too early defeats Cow and allocates on every call.

body_md: `AsRef<str>` accepts `String`, `&str`, and `Box<str>` in one signature. Write `fn open<P: AsRef<Path>>(p: P)` style APIs so callers pass whatever they hold. Prefer `AsRef` over concrete `&String` params.
hook: Take &String and you annoy every caller — take AsRef instead.

quiz.explain: AsRef accepts many owned and borrowed forms of the same data.
options: Callers can pass String or &str
It forces callers to clone first
It only accepts 'static strings
It makes the function run faster
quiz.q: Why use AsRef<str> parameters?

takeaway: Accept AsRef in public APIs so callers can pass owned or borrowed values.
trap: Taking &String blocks &str callers for no benefit; use AsRef or &str.

body_md: `Borrow<str>` powers `HashMap<String>` lookups by `&str`. Because `String: Borrow<str>` plus `str: Eq + Hash`, `map.get("key")` works without allocating. Keep key types Borrow-compatible.
hook: HashMap<String> looked up by &str with zero alloc — Borrow magic.

quiz.explain: Borrow lets owned map keys be queried with borrowed equivalents.
options: Looking up String keys with a &str
Storing &str keys without lifetimes
Sorting entries by key on insert
Mutating keys in place after insert
quiz.q: What does Borrow enable for maps?

takeaway: Rely on Borrow so owned-key maps support cheap borrowed lookups.
trap: Custom keys without a Borrow impl force wasteful owned lookups.

body_md: Model failures as enums with `thiserror`: each variant carries context and `#[error("... {0}")]` renders messages. Derive `Error` plus `Debug`. Use for library APIs where callers match on cases.
code:
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
enum DbErr {
    #[error("missing user {0}")]
    Missing(String),
    #[error(transparent)]
    Io(#[from] std::io::Error),
}
hook: One error enum to rule every failure in your library.

quiz.explain: thiserror derives Error for enums with formatted messages per variant.
options: Deriving Error for your typed enums
Replacing Result with a dynamic error
Catching panics and converting them
Logging warnings when errors occur
quiz.q: What is thiserror for?

takeaway: Derive typed library errors with thiserror so callers can match precisely.
trap: Using stringly errors in libraries prevents callers from handling cases.

body_md: `anyhow::Result` plus `.context("loading config")` adds a breadcrumb trail to app errors. The `?` propagates, context explains what you were doing. Print with `{:?}` for the full chain in logs.
hook: anyhow's .context() says which file failed and why
output: Err: loading app config (caused by: No such file or directory)

quiz.explain: context attaches what-you-were-doing notes to propagated errors.
options: A note saying what you were doing
A retry of the failed operation
A conversion to a typed error enum
A hidden, quieter error message
quiz.q: What does anyhow context add?

takeaway: Attach anyhow context at app boundaries to make failures easy to diagnose.
trap: Adding context inside tight loops buries the root cause under noise.

body_md: `map` transforms, `filter` keeps matches, `filter_map` does both. They are lazy until consumed. Chain then `collect()`: `(1..10).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).map(|x| x * x)`. Name closures for clarity.
hook: Filter then map in one pass — no temp vectors needed.

quiz.explain: Adapters are lazy and fuse into one pass when consumed.
options: Each adapter builds its own Vec first
Eagerly, as soon as they're chained
Lazily, once a consumer pulls items
filter runs at once, map runs later
quiz.q: When do map and filter execute?

takeaway: Chain lazy adapters and consume once to process data in a single pass.
trap: Forgetting the final collect means the adapter chain never runs at all.

body_md: `fold` reduces to one value with an accumulator: `iter.fold(0, |acc, x| acc + x)`. Use it for sums, histograms, or building maps. Prefer `sum()` and `product()` shorthands when they fit.
code:
let sum = (1..=4).fold(0, |acc, x| acc + x);
let prod: i32 = (1..=4).product();
hook: Sum, count, histogram — fold turns many values into one.

quiz.explain: fold threads an accumulator through every element to one result.
options: Filters elements into a new iterator
Reduces all items to one value
Pairs up items from two iterators
Flattens nested iterators into one
quiz.q: What does fold do?

takeaway: Use fold to reduce iterators into a single summary value or collection.
trap: Folding with a shared mutable accumulator across threads causes data races.

body_md: `enumerate` adds indices, `zip` pairs two iterators and stops at the shorter. Perfect for progress bars and pairwise diffs: `for (i, (a, b)) in xs.iter().zip(ys).enumerate()`. Check lengths first if truncation matters.
hook: Need index plus two values at once? Zip meets enumerate.

quiz.explain: zip stops at the shorter iterator while enumerate adds indices.
options: zip pads the shorter side with None
zip stops at the shorter iterator
zip panics when lengths differ
zip cycles the shorter one again
quiz.q: What happens when zipped iterators differ in length?

takeaway: Pair iterators with zip and enumerate but verify lengths when truncation matters.
trap: Silent zip truncation drops trailing data when inputs differ in length.

body_md: Collect into `Result<Vec<_>, E>` to fail fast: `list.iter().map(parse).collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()?`. First `Err` short-circuits the whole collection. Use for validating batches of inputs at once.
hook: Parse ten strings, fail on the first bad one — one collect.

quiz.explain: Collecting to Result short-circuits on the first error.
options: Returns the first Err and stops
Skips every Err and keeps the Oks
Collects every Err into the Vec
Panics as soon as a parse fails
quiz.q: What does collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>> do on error?

takeaway: Collect fallible maps into Result to validate whole batches with early exit.
trap: Collecting into Vec then checking loses which element failed first.

body_md: Elision has three rules: each input `&` gets its own lifetime, one input lifetime flows to outputs, and `&self` dominates methods. `fn f(a: &str) -> &str` works; `fn f(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str` needs annotations.
hook: Three elision rules explain 90 percent of lifetime errors.

quiz.explain: With two input borrows the compiler cannot guess which flows to output.
options: Elision can't pick which input to tie to
A fn can't return a borrowed &str at all
&str outputs always need 'static
It compiles; elision handles two inputs
quiz.q: Why does fn pick(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str fail?

takeaway: Learn the three elision rules so you annotate only truly ambiguous signatures.
trap: Annotating every lifetime by hand hides the simple elided shape.

body_md: **HRTB** `for<'a>` means works for *any* lifetime: `fn f(x: &dyn Fn(&str))`. Needed when a closure must accept fresh borrows each call. You will meet it in async trait bounds and higher-order functions.
hook: A closure that works for ANY lifetime? That is HRTB.

quiz.explain: HRTB expresses bounds that must hold for every possible lifetime.
options: It must hold for every lifetime 'a
It loops over each borrow at runtime
'a is fixed to the caller's scope
'a is always treated as 'static
quiz.q: What does for<'a> in a bound mean?

takeaway: Recognize higher-ranked bounds when closures must accept any fresh borrow.
trap: Forcing one concrete lifetime where any-lifetime is needed over-constrains callers.

body_md: `dyn Trait` erases concrete type for heterogeneous lists: `Vec<Box<dyn Draw>>`. You pay a vtable plus no inlining. Keep trait objects object-safe (no generics) and prefer generics on hot paths.
hook: A vector of different types? Trait objects erase the difference.
output: shapes.len() → 0 (each element may differ in type)

quiz.explain: dyn Trait calls go through a vtable pointer, which costs an indirection and usually prevents inlining.
options: A vtable call that blocks inlining
One monomorphized copy per type
A garbage-collection header per value
Nothing; it's the same as generics
quiz.q: What is the cost of dyn Trait?

takeaway: Use trait objects for heterogeneous collections and generics for hot paths.
trap: Putting non-object-safe generic methods on a dyn trait breaks compilation.

body_md: `Send` means safe to move across threads, `Sync` means safe to share by reference. `Rc` is neither; `Arc` is both when `T` is. The compiler checks bounds on `spawn` and channels — trust the errors.
hook: Send versus Sync in one sentence each — finally clear.
output: OK — thread returns 3 via join; no output

quiz.explain: Send allows moving ownership across threads while Sync allows sharing refs.
options: They control how futures are polled
Send: safe to move; Sync: safe to share
They fix a type's layout in memory
Send: safe to share; Sync: safe to move
quiz.q: What do Send and Sync guarantee?

takeaway: Let Send and Sync bounds guide which types can cross thread boundaries.
trap: Wrapping Rc in Arc or sending raw pointers across threads breaks safety.

body_md: `Arc<T>` shares ownership across threads with atomic counts. Clone the `Arc` (cheap counter bump), not the inner data. Pair with `Mutex` or atomics for mutation. Watch for reference cycles in graphs.
hook: Share data across threads without copying — Arc clone is cheap.

quiz.explain: Arc clone bumps the atomic count without copying inner data.
options: Deep-copies the data for the thread
Bumps an atomic count; no data copy
Moves the data onto a fresh heap slot
Locks a mutex, then copies the value
quiz.q: What does Arc::clone do?

takeaway: Share immutable data across threads with cheap Arc clones around it.
trap: Cloning inner data instead of the Arc copies megabytes on every spawn.

body_md: A `Mutex` **poisons** when a holder panics — `lock()` returns `Err` carrying the guard. Usually the data is still fine: call `.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` to recover deliberately after auditing state.
hook: Mutex poisoned after a panic — crash or keep going?

quiz.explain: Poisoning signals a panic while holding the lock and lock returns Err.
options: A holder panicked, so lock() gives Err
The mutex was dropped while still locked
Two threads have deadlocked on the lock
The guarded data was freed while locked
quiz.q: What is mutex poisoning?

takeaway: Handle poisoned mutexes deliberately by recovering only after auditing state.
trap: Blindly unwrapping lock results turns recoverable poison into a second crash.

body_md: `mpsc::channel` moves values between threads; `recv` blocks. For many producers, clone the `Sender`. When you need timeouts or multiple inputs, use `crossbeam::select!` or check `try_recv` in a loop.
hook: Threads talking past each other? Give them a channel.

quiz.explain: Cloned senders allow many producers feeding one receiver.
options: Clone the Sender once per producer
Clone the Receiver for each thread
Wrap the Sender in a Mutex first
Use sync_channel; mpsc is one-to-one
quiz.q: How do you get multiple producers on mpsc?

takeaway: Connect threads with channels and clone senders for multi-producer flows.
trap: Blocking recv on the main thread with no sender left deadlocks forever.

body_md: **Scoped threads** (`thread::scope`) borrow stack data safely — no `Arc` needed. The scope joins all children before returning, so borrows cannot outlive the parent. Prefer scopes for fork-join parallelism.
hook: Borrow stack data in threads with zero Arc — scoped threads.
output: error[E0502]: cannot borrow `v` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable

quiz.explain: Scopes guarantee children join before borrows expire.
options: The scope joins them before returning
They copy all locals onto their stack
They run on the caller's own thread
Borrows in threads are unchecked
quiz.q: Why can scoped threads borrow locals?

takeaway: Use scoped threads for fork-join work that borrows local data safely.
trap: Spawning detached threads that borrow locals escapes the borrow checker illegally.

body_md: `DerefMut` enables `*box_ref = new_val` through smart pointers. `MutexGuard` uses it so `guard.field = x` writes through the lock. Do not implement `DerefMut` unless shared mutation is the point.
hook: DerefMut lets you assign through a smart pointer

quiz.explain: DerefMut powers mutable access through smart pointer wrappers.
options: Writing through it, as in *b = 10
Cloning the value on every write
Mutating through raw pointers only
Freezing the pointee against writes
quiz.q: What does DerefMut enable?

takeaway: Use DerefMut for pointer-like mutation and avoid it on plain domain types.
trap: DerefMut on value types lets callers silently mutate internals.

body_md: Prefer `TryFrom` for fallible conversions: `impl TryFrom<&str> for Port` returns `Result`. Use `?` at call sites. Reserve panicking `From` for truly infallible mappings like widening integers.
hook: Conversion can fail? Then From is the wrong trait.

quiz.explain: TryFrom signals failure with Result instead of panicking.
options: When the conversion might fail
When the types share a layout
Whenever From would be too slow
When converting between references
quiz.q: When should you use TryFrom?

takeaway: Model fallible conversions with TryFrom so failures surface as Results.
trap: Panicking inside From for invalid input turns bad data into crashes.
